questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman presented with fever, coryza, and a rash. She was in the first trimester of pregnancy. She had not traveled overseas in the last year. She was a college student in a rural area. She reports full vaccination. On examination her temperature was 37.1°C. She had a widespread macular pink rash.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely infective cause?
questions.explanation: Parvovirus B19 Several of the options could cause fever and a rash; however, measles and rubella are now rare in routine clinical practice due to vaccination. These would be possible diagnoses, particularly if the woman were unvaccinated, had traveled overseas, or there was an epidemiologic link to a measles outbreak. Secondary syphilis could cause a rash and fever but not upper respiratory symptoms. Acute Q fever would more usually be associated with cough and myalgia rather than coryza and does not typically cause a rash. Parvovirus B19 is a ubiquitous infection which is frequently asymptomatic but can cause these symptoms. Moreover, identifying acute parvovirus infection in this context is important because of the associated risk of hydrops fetalis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q23

questions.stem: A full-term neonate was seen on the postnatal ward and referred for an urgent neonatal consultation. Her mother had recently entered the country as a refugee and had presented in labor, having not received any antenatal care. On examination, the baby was found to have bilateral cataracts, microcephaly, and sensorineural deafness.
questions.lead_in: What virus is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Rubella The greatest risk of severe congenital disease occurs if the mother acquires rubella in the 1st trimester of pregnancy. Other features of the congenital rubella syndrome include cardiac defects, hepatomegaly or hepatitis, bone lesions, and developmental delay. Congenital varicella syndrome is rare but usually occurs in neonates whose mother acquired infection in the 2nd trimester and is characterized by cicatricial skin lesions (scars), limb hypoplasia, and ocular defects. Parvovirus B19 is associated with fetal hydrops, although most intrauterine parvovirus infections are not adversely affected. Evidence of parvovirus as a teratogen is lacking. CMV is asymptomatic at birth in 90% of children born with congenital CMV; although microcephaly, deafness, and visual loss due to chorioretinitis are associated with CMV , cataracts are not typical and suggest an alternative etiology. Measles is not associated with congenital disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q12

questions.question: Name the congenital infection most associated with each of the following findings.
questions.model_answer: a) Osteitis – congenital syphilis. b) Periventricular calcifications – CMV. c) Scarring (cicatricial skin lesions) – varicella-zoster virus. d) Heart failure – parvovirus B19 (hydrops from fetal anemia). e) Cataracts – rubella.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the CMV/periventricular-calcification link is in this chapter; the syphilis, VZV, parvovirus, and rubella associations rest on standard congenital-infection (TORCH) teaching (Red Book).

questions.question: Match each congenital syndrome finding to the causative infection: osteitis, periventricular calcifications, cicatricial scarring, congestive heart failure, cataracts, dactylitis, salt-and-pepper retinopathy, microcephaly, hypoplastic lower limbs, myocarditis.
questions.question_raw: Match the congenital syndrome to the infection: Osteitis, Periventricular calcifications, Scarring (cicatrical), CHF, Cataracts, Dactylitis, Salt and pepper retinopathy, Microcephaly, Hypoplastic lower limbs, Myocarditis

parts.text: Match the congenital syndrome to the infection

parts_raw.text: Match the congenital syndrome to the infection

questions.model_answer: a) Osteitis/osteochondritis - congenital syphilis. Periventricular calcifications - cytomegalovirus (Toxoplasma calcifications are diffuse/scattered). Cicatricial scarring - congenital varicella syndrome. Congestive heart failure (hydrops from severe anemia) - parvovirus B19. Cataracts - rubella. Dactylitis - congenital syphilis. Salt-and-pepper retinopathy - rubella (also syphilis). Microcephaly - cytomegalovirus and Zika virus. Hypoplastic lower limbs - congenital varicella syndrome. Myocarditis - enteroviruses/coxsackievirus B (also parvovirus B19).
questions.beyond_mandell: Standard congenital infection teaching (Mandell congenital/perinatal infection chapters).

cohort_answer.text: Osteitis - Syphilis. Periventricular calcifications - CMV (also Toxo, rubella, HSV, zika). Scarring (cicatrical) - Varicella. Heart failure (congenital heart disease) - Parvovirus B19. Cataracts - Rubella (also syphilis, toxo). Dactylitis - Syphilis (early but rare). Salt and Pepper Retinopathy - Rubella/syphilis. Microcephaly - CMV (most common), rubella, Zika, toxo. Hypoplastic lower limbs - Varicella. Myocarditis - Parvovirus B19, enterovirus D70, Coxsackie A24

questions.question: Match each congenital finding to the congenital infection with which it is classically associated.
questions.model_answer: a) Osteitis (osteochondritis, periostitis, "Wimberger sign"): congenital syphilis (Treponema pallidum). b) Periventricular (periventricular/subependymal) calcifications: congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV). c) Cicatricial scarring (dermatomal skin scarring, limb hypoplasia): congenital varicella syndrome (VZV). d) Heart failure/hydrops from myocarditis or severe anemia: parvovirus B19 (also myocarditis in rubella, syphilis, and Chagas disease). e) Cataracts (with microphthalmia, plus PDA/pulmonic stenosis, sensorineural deafness): congenital rubella syndrome.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only cataracts (rubella) is grounded in this chapter (Table 152.1, p. 2009); the osteitis-syphilis, periventricular calcification-CMV, scarring-VZV, and heart-failure-parvovirus B19 associations are standard TORCH teaching from the respective Mandell chapters, not this one.

questions.question: For each of the following congenital findings, identify the most likely infectious cause: periventricular calcifications; cutaneous scarring; heart failure; osteitis; cataracts.
questions.question_raw: PM 11. What is the most likely infectious cause of the following congenital findings? periventricular calcifications (0.5); cutaneous scarring (0.5); heart failure (0.5); Osteitis (0.5); Cataracts (0.5)

parts.text: Identify the infectious cause for each congenital finding.

parts_raw.text: Identify the infectious cause for each congenital finding

questions.model_answer: (1) Periventricular calcifications – CMV. (2) Cutaneous scarring – varicella-zoster virus (congenital varicella). (3) Heart failure – parvovirus B19 (hydrops from fetal anemia). (4) Osteitis – congenital syphilis. (5) Cataracts – rubella.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the CMV/periventricular-calcification association is in this chapter; the VZV, parvovirus, syphilis, and rubella associations rest on standard congenital-infection (TORCH) teaching (Red Book).

cohort_answer.text: Periventricular calcifications - CMV (widespread/intracranial calcifications more suggest Toxoplasmosis). Cutaneous scarring - VZV. Heart failure - Parvovirus (>>>Rubella). Osteitis - Syphilis (saber shin). Cataracts - Rubella.
